stories.title: Generations at the forge
stories.summary: The Harrisons’ forge on Church Street made and mended almost everything the village needed.
stories.body:
For generations the village forge was where things got made and mended. Its blacksmiths shod horses, but they also made cart wheels, gates and ironmongery for farms and households all over the parish.

The forge was on Church Street and was run by the Harrison family. A photograph from 1926 shows the blacksmith at work at Harrison’s Forge, and decades later, when the village’s old fire pump was restored, one of its wooden wheels was repaired at “Harrison’s Church Street Blacksmiths”.

The forge also shows how village trades changed with the times. A Bulletin exhibition notice describes a shop where you could have your horse shod, your wireless accumulator charged or your bike brakes fixed, all in one place.
stories.source: East Hendred Bulletin, Spring 2016 (no. 144) and Winter 2015 (no. 143), East Hendred Parish Council; Hendred Museum, ‘The Fire Pump’, https://www.hendredmuseum.org.uk/fire-pump

stories.title: The day the evacuees came
stories.summary: On 1 September 1939 London schoolboys from West Ham arrived to sit out the war in the village.
stories.body:
On 1 September 1939, two days before Britain declared war on Germany, a party of evacuee children from London arrived in East Hendred. Among them were boys from Cave Road School in West Ham, in the East End.

Their arrival changed village life overnight. The village school suddenly had to make room for them, and accounts suggest local children and evacuees took turns, with the village children in school in the mornings.

Some stayed on. A 2006 Bulletin mentions a village family who first came to Hendred as evacuees, and decades after the war the Bulletin was still appealing for former evacuees to get in touch for a reunion.
stories.people: Boys of Cave Road School, West Ham
stories.source: East Hendred Bulletin, Summer 2004 (no. 102); Winter 2015 (no. 143); Autumn 2006 (no. 107); Hendred Museum WW2 exhibition (2025–26)

stories.title: Halfpennies at Wilkins
stories.summary: Older villagers remember spending their halfpennies at Wilkins Shop.
stories.body:
Ask older villagers about childhood treats and you may hear about Wilkins Shop, where children spent their halfpennies.

In a village with no through road, the shop was one of the places where everyone’s day crossed. Memories like this were gathered for the Bulletin’s local history exhibitions, and the Hendred Museum would like to hear from anyone who remembers what Wilkins sold, or who ran it.
stories.source: East Hendred Bulletin, Spring 2016 (no. 144)

stories.title: A family of carpenters
stories.summary: Joseph Hunt, born 1771, began several generations of Hunt carpenters in the village.
stories.body:
Joseph Hunt was born in East Hendred in 1771. He is the first of his family to be recorded in the village as a carpenter, and several generations of Hunts followed him into the trade.

In a village of timber-framed cottages, barns and farm carts, a carpenter’s work never ran out.
stories.source: ‘The Hunts of East Hendred’, family history website, https://freepages.rootsweb.com/~hendred/genealogy/Hunts.htm

stories.title: The parson who wrote home
stories.summary: Rector George Woodward’s letters to his uncle give a rare look inside a Georgian parsonage.
stories.body:
George Woodward was rector of East Hendred from the 1750s until he died on 5 May 1790. He lived at the rectory opposite the church: a timber-framed house later enlarged in red brick, with remarkable yew hedges in its garden.

Between 1753 and 1761 he wrote a long run of letters to his uncle. They are mostly about himself and his family rather than the village, but they give a rare, informal picture of a Georgian country parson’s household. He wrote without paragraphs, in one long flow.

He left a mark in the church too. Among the church plate, a flagon and alms dish are inscribed ‘Ex dono Geo. Woodward Rector 1783’: a gift from the rector in 1783.

The letters were edited by Donald Gibson and published in 1982 as A Parson in the Vale of White Horse.
stories.place: The rectory, opposite St Augustine’s Church
stories.source: D. Gibson (ed.), A Parson in the Vale of White Horse: George Woodward’s Letters from East Hendred 1753–1761 (Alan Sutton, 1982); ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302; J. Foster, Alumni Oxonienses 1715–1886, vol. 4, p. 414

stories.title: Keeping the faceless clock
stories.summary: Made in 1525, wound by hand for centuries, overhauled in 1961 and restored again for its 500th birthday.
stories.body:
St Augustine’s clock was made in 1525 by John Seymour of Wantage, whose name and the date are still inscribed on part of the works. It has no dial and no hands. It tells the time by striking, and every three hours from nine in the morning it plays a hymn tune, the Angels’ Song, usually credited to Orlando Gibbons.

For centuries someone climbed the tower to wind it by hand every day. In 1961 Arthur Harrison overhauled it, and the Hendred Museum says it has kept very good time since.

In 2024, ahead of its 500th birthday, the clock was restored again and given automatic winding. The village celebrated Clock500 in 2025 with tower tours, and the BBC reported on the clock still keeping the village on time after five centuries.
stories.people: John Seymour of Wantage; Arthur Harrison; Simon Gilchrist (horologist)
stories.source: ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302; Hendred Museum, ‘Points of interest’, https://www.hendredmuseum.org.uk/points-of-interest; ‘East Hendred’, Wikipedia (citing BBC News, ‘Oxfordshire clock still keeping village on time after 500 years’, 28 May 2025); C.F.C. Beeson, Clockmaking in Oxfordshire 1400–1850 (3rd edn, 1989), p. 20

stories.title: The physicist on Cat Street
stories.summary: William Penney, leader of Britain’s atomic programme, lived at Orchard House and took the village’s name.
stories.body:
William Penney (1909–1991) was the mathematician and physicist who led Britain’s atomic weapons programme. He worked at Los Alamos during the Second World War, and later headed the Atomic Weapons Research Establishment and the UK Atomic Energy Authority, whose Harwell site sits on the edge of the parish.

He made his home at Orchard House on Cat Street. When he was made a life peer in 1967 he took the title Baron Penney, of East Hendred, and he died in the village on 3 March 1991.

In later life he admitted to qualms about his work, though he maintained it had been necessary. A blue plaque was unveiled at Orchard House on 8 August 2014.
stories.source: ‘William Penney, Baron Penney’, Wikipedia; Oxfordshire Blue Plaques Board, ‘William Penney’, http://oxonblueplaques.org.uk/plaques/penney.html

stories.title: Ghosts without feet
stories.summary: Civil War soldiers seen in a village cottage, but only from the ankles up.
stories.body:
After one of the Civil War battles at Newbury in the 1640s, Parliamentarian soldiers are said to have been billeted in East Hendred.

Three centuries later, in the 1940s, people in one village cottage reported ghostly Roundhead soldiers, visible only from the ankles up. The explanation offered was simple: the floor had been raised since the 1600s, so the soldiers walked on the old floor level, their feet hidden beneath the new one.

The story doesn’t record which cottage it was.
stories.source: Royal Berkshire History, ‘East Hendred’ (Nash Ford Publishing, 2001), https://www.berkshirehistory.com/villages/easthendred.html

stories.title: The cloth fairs of the Golden Mile
stories.summary: Tradition says Hendred’s medieval cloth fairs were held on a green lane called the Golden Mile.
stories.body:
In the 15th century East Hendred grew rich on cloth, rich enough to be called a town. Brasses in the church remember its wool merchants: the brothers Henry and Roger Eldysley (Roger died in 1439), shown with their merchants’ marks, and William Whitwey (1479), described in Latin as a draper and woolman.

Village tradition says the cloth fairs were held on a green lane known as the Golden Mile, and links certain grass terraces in the centre of the village with the trade. Nobody has proved it, but the name has stuck.

There were real fairs too. In 1415 Henry V granted the Prior of Sheen a Tuesday market and two fairs here, around St Augustine’s day (26 May) and St Katherine’s (25 November). They never really flourished.
stories.people: Henry and Roger Eldysley; William Whitwey
stories.source: ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302

stories.title: A king’s revenge at Cwichelm’s mound
stories.summary: A botched assassination, a royal revenge, and a king who may or may not lie under Scutchamer Knob.
stories.body:
Cwichelm was a 7th-century king of the Gewisse, the people who became the West Saxons. The historian Bede says that around 626 Cwichelm sent an assassin to kill King Edwin of Northumbria. The attempt failed.

A much later chronicle, written at St Albans in the 13th century, claims Edwin took his revenge by killing Cwichelm at the mound on the downs that bears his name: Cwichelm’s barrow, now Scutchamer Knob. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle tells a different story, in which Cwichelm was baptised at Dorchester in 636 and died the same year.

The mound is older than either king. It is an early Iron Age barrow, and digs have found no burial. The legend of a king beneath it has lasted anyway.
stories.people: King Cwichelm of the Gewisse; King Edwin of Northumbria
stories.source: ‘Cwichelm of Wessex’, Wikipedia (citing Bede and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle); Royal Berkshire History, ‘East Hendred’; ‘Scutchamer Knob’, Wikipedia; Historic England list entry 1006312

stories.title: The Danes take a dare
stories.summary: In 1006 a Viking army marched to Cwichelm’s barrow to defy a prophecy, then went home anyway.
stories.body:
In the winter of 1006 a Danish army raiding Wessex marched up to Cwichelm’s barrow on the Berkshire Downs. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle explains why: it had long been said that if they ever reached the mound, they would never get back to the sea.

They reached it, waited there as if daring the prophecy to come true, and then went back to the sea by another way. The Chronicle’s account of that year records the barrow by its old name, Cwichelmeshlæw.
stories.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal for 1006 (as summarised in ‘Scutchamer Knob’, Wikipedia, and the Victoria County History, Berkshire vol. 4, p. 294)

stories.title: The job that let MPs quit
stories.summary: For 77 years, MPs who wanted to leave Parliament became ‘Steward of the Manor of East Hendred’.
stories.body:
MPs can’t simply resign. Instead, they take a nominal paid office under the Crown, which disqualifies them from the Commons. Today that office is the Chiltern Hundreds. From 1763 to 1840, one of the offices used was Steward of the Manor of East Hendred, the King’s Manor.

Dozens of MPs passed through the job, and the reasons tell the politics of Georgian Britain: to stand for another seat, to make way for a patron’s favourite, to become an ambassador, to express support for the radical John Wilkes, even because of ill health. In 1765 one MP stood down so that Edmund Burke could be brought into Parliament.

The Crown actually sold the manor in 1823, but nobody noticed, and stewards kept being appointed for another seventeen years.
stories.source: ‘List of stewards of the Manor of East Hendred’, Wikipedia; ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302 (stewardship as ‘an office of honour and profit’)

stories.title: Wynflæd’s lawsuit at the mound
stories.summary: Around 990 a woman took a land dispute to the king, and the case was settled at Cwichelm’s barrow.
stories.body:
Scutchamer Knob wasn’t only a legend. For centuries it was where the shire court met in the open air, and one of England’s best-recorded Anglo-Saxon lawsuits was settled there.

Around 990, a woman named Wynflæd claimed that a man called Leofwine had seized land at Hagbourne and Bradfield which his father had given her in exchange for land at Datchet. She took the case to King Æthelred and produced an impressive line of witnesses, including the archbishop of Canterbury, the king’s mother, and the abbesses of Winchester and Reading. More than half of her witnesses were women.

The shire court at Cwichelm’s barrow reached a compromise. Leofwine handed back the land and paid compensation instead of facing an oath against him, and Wynflæd had to return the gold and silver his father had given her. Why she had them is never explained.
stories.source: Charter S 1454, Electronic Sawyer, https://esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/1454.html; A. Rabin, essay on S 1454, Old English Newsletter 41.3; Historic England list entry 1006312

stories.title: The Devil’s spadeful
stories.summary: Some said the Devil made Scutchamer Knob by scraping the mud off his spade.
stories.body:
Not everyone believed a king lay under Scutchamer Knob. An old local tale gives the credit to the Devil.

In one version he dug a great ditch along the downs in a single night, then climbed to the top and scraped the earth off his spade, and the scrapings became the mound. In another he fancied himself a ploughman and cut a furrow along the hillside; when his ploughshare clogged, he scraped it clean and tossed the soil over the Ridgeway.

Others said the mound held King Cwichelm, or the soldiers who died with him. The Devil’s version is the only one that explains why there’s nobody inside.
stories.source: Dark Oxfordshire, ‘Moots and Burials at Scutchamer Knob’, https://www.darkoxfordshire.co.uk/explore/moots-and-burials-at-scutchamer-knob/; The Modern Antiquarian, ‘Scutchamer Knob’ folklore posts (quoting a Victorian account)

stories.title: The village fire pump
stories.summary: After a ‘Great Fire of Hendred’, the parish bought a horse-drawn fire pump in 1831. It still survives.
stories.body:
In a village of thatched cottages, fire was a constant fear. After a series of disastrous fires, one remembered as the Great Fire of Hendred and mentioned in the House of Commons, the parish overseers bought a horse-drawn fire pump in 1831.

The parish ran its own brigade, with a captain and an engineer. When the alarm went up, pumpers and ‘bucket men’ were gathered, at least two pumping on each side. Each wore a leather arm band with a numbered copper tag, and only those with arm bands were paid, by the hour. Fifteen-foot rakes rode along the side for dragging burning thatch off roofs.

The pump was last used in earnest at a fire in 1938, when the Wantage fire brigade needed its help to draw water from the stream. After 1945 it found a gentler job, watering a new cricket pitch during a drought. Restored by volunteers, it is now on display at Snells Hall.
stories.place: Snells Hall (display); originally the village pound near Champs Chapel
stories.source: Hendred Museum, ‘The Fire Pump’, https://www.hendredmuseum.org.uk/fire-pump

stories.title: The feast on the green
stories.summary: Every Whitsun the village held a four-day feast on the green, perhaps a survival of a medieval fair.
stories.body:
In 1415 Henry V granted East Hendred a market and two fairs. The market faded before the Reformation, but something of the fairs lived on. By the early 20th century the village held a yearly feast on the green, starting on the Sunday before Whitsun and running for the next three days. Historians think it may descend from the old St Augustine’s fair.

Travelling showmen made the rounds of these feasts. Neighbouring Harwell remembers that Isaac Pryor’s travelling fair came over from East Hendred, with Dolloware’s roundabouts, a coconut shy, hoopla, home-made flapjacks and ‘ha’penny squirters’ that the lads used to frighten the girls.
stories.source: ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302; ‘The Whit Monday Feast’, Harwell: Village for a Thousand Years, https://village4a1000years.uk/1945-1985-2/the-whit-monday-feast/

stories.title: A prayer for the kings
stories.summary: In 1274 a villager held his land in return for saying the Lord’s Prayer every day for England’s kings.
stories.body:
Medieval land was usually held in return for rent or labour. In 1274 one villager, Ralph son of Thomas de Hendred, held a strip of land called a virgate on a gentler condition: he had to say a Pater Noster, the Lord’s Prayer, every day for the souls of the kings of England.

The land passed down his family for more than a century. Its name survived even longer: a road called Paternoster Bank could still be identified in the early 1700s.
stories.people: Ralph son of Thomas de Hendred
stories.source: ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302 (citing Cal. Inq. p.m. Edw. I and Ashmole, Antiquities of Berkshire)

stories.title: Court under a tree
stories.summary: The King’s Manor court once met under a tree in the village, and had the right to a pillory.
stories.body:
When Henry V granted the King’s Manor to the monks of Sheen in 1415, he also gave them the right to punish petty offenders: the right to a pillory and a tumbrel (a ducking or cucking stool), and to control the quality of bread and ale sold in the village.

The manor court kept meeting long after the monks had gone. In the mid-1600s it was held in the open air, under a tree in the village. By the early 1800s it had moved indoors, to a cottage just opposite Champs Chapel.
stories.place: The village, and a cottage opposite Champs Chapel
stories.source: ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302 (citing the Parliamentary Survey of Berkshire and BL Add. MS 9409)

stories.title: Lavinia Smith’s museum of village life
stories.summary: An American former nun collected old farm tools and household things and opened a village museum in 1933.
stories.body:
Lavinia Smith was born in Portsmouth, Ohio, in 1871. After teaching in America she came to England, joined the Anglican Community of St Mary the Virgin at Wantage, and taught in its schools before leaving the order. Around 1920 she bought Downside, a Tudor house on the Newbury Road in East Hendred, where she lived with her sister Frances.

She began collecting the tools and household objects of old village life, keeping careful records of who gave each piece, and on Whit Sunday 1933 she opened her own museum of agricultural and village antiquities. Schoolchildren were especially welcome.

She died in 1944. Her collection, several hundred objects, went to the Museum of English Rural Life in Reading in 1951, where it is still known as the Lavinia Smith collection.
stories.source: ‘Lavinia Smith’, Wikipedia; Museum of English Rural Life, ‘Sister Lavinia’, https://merl.reading.ac.uk/?p=19133; MERL 51 Voices, Object 22

stories.title: The scholar of Hendred House
stories.summary: Charles Eyston, a Catholic antiquary, wrote a history of Glastonbury Abbey and was loved for his charity.
stories.body:
Charles Eyston was born at Hendred House in 1667 and died there in 1721. As a Catholic he was barred from public life, so he turned to scholarship.

His history of Glastonbury, A Little Monument to the Once Famous Abbey and Borough of Glastonbury, was published by his friend the Oxford antiquary Thomas Hearne in 1722. Another manuscript, A Poor Little Monument to All the Old Pious Dissolved Foundations of England, a history of the monasteries closed at the Reformation, stayed unpublished in the family library.

Hearne remembered him as ‘so charitable to the poor that he is lamented by all who knew anything of him’. Charles and his wife Winefrid had eleven children, and several of their daughters became nuns.
stories.source: ‘Charles Eyston’, Wikipedia (incorporating the Catholic Encyclopedia, 1913, and Hearne’s Reliquiae Hearnianae)

stories.title: Racehorses on the downs
stories.summary: East Hendred’s stables trained a Derby favourite in 1951 and a Grand National winner in 1987.
stories.body:
The chalk downs above the village make fine gallops, and East Hendred has been a racing village.

In 1951 Ki Ming, trained in East Hendred, won the 2,000 Guineas at Newmarket and started favourite for the Derby, though he couldn’t last the longer distance at Epsom.

Thirty-six years later the village had a winner of the most famous race of all. Maori Venture, trained by Andy Turnell at his East Hendred stables and owned by Jim Joel, won the 1987 Grand National at 28 to 1. He was retired straight after the race.
stories.people: Ki Ming; Maori Venture; Andy Turnell (trainer); Jim Joel (owner)
stories.source: ‘Maori Venture’ and ‘1987 Grand National’, Wikipedia; Racing Post obituary of Andy Turnell; ‘Ki Ming’, Wikipedia; Hendred Museum media archive (slideshows of both)

stories.title: Two eggs, lightly poached
stories.summary: Statesman Roy Jenkins lived in East Hendred for decades and is buried in Cat Street cemetery.
stories.body:
Roy Jenkins (1920–2003), Chancellor of the Exchequer, Home Secretary, President of the European Commission and a founder of the SDP, made his home in East Hendred.

He died there on 5 January 2003 after a heart attack. His last words, to his wife, are reported as: ‘Two eggs, please, lightly poached.’

He is buried in the Cat Street cemetery, in the village where he spent the second half of his life.
stories.people: Roy Jenkins, Baron Jenkins of Hillhead (1920–2003)
stories.source: ‘Roy Jenkins’, Wikipedia (last words cited to his biography)

stories.title: The airfield on the downs
stories.summary: A third of RAF Harwell lay in East Hendred parish. It was bombed in 1940–41 and launched D-Day’s pathfinders.
stories.body:
RAF Harwell took its name from the neighbouring village, but the airfield straddled three parishes: most of it in Chilton, about a third in East Hendred, and the smallest part in Harwell.

Its bombers flew leaflet raids and bombing missions, and the airfield was attacked many times by the Luftwaffe between August 1940 and September 1941. Later in the war it became a base for airborne forces, and on the night of 5 June 1944 the first pathfinder aircraft of the D-Day landings took off from Harwell.

In 1946 the airfield became the Atomic Energy Research Establishment, which brought new families and new work to the village, and grew into today’s Harwell Campus.
stories.place: Harwell Campus, east of the village
stories.source: ‘RAF Harwell’, Wikipedia; Hendred Museum WW2 exhibition (2025–26)

stories.title: The bell called Gabriel
stories.summary: St Augustine’s six bells span the Reformation and the Civil War, and one is named Gabriel.
stories.body:
The six bells in St Augustine’s tower carry their own history in their inscriptions.

The oldest, the fourth, is dedicated to St Anne, ‘Sancta Anna ora pro nobis’, and was cast before the Reformation. The third simply says ‘Feare God, 1647’, made in the middle of the Civil War. The treble was made by Ellis and Henry Knight in 1674, and the tenor announces: ‘Samuel Knight made mee Gabriel my name to bee 1689.’
stories.people: Ellis, Henry and Samuel Knight, bellfounders
stories.source: ‘Parishes: East Hendred’, in A History of the County of Berkshire, vol. 4, ed. W. Page and P.H. Ditchfield (Victoria County History, 1924), pp. 294–302, https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/berks/vol4/pp294-302; Hendred Museum, ‘Points of interest’
